documentation: The distributable surface every published workspace receives downstream: its `exports` map, its `files` allowlist, and the build wiring that produces the artifacts both point at. Corvidae deliberately carries none of these — `scripts/workspace-contract.test.ts` pins every library's `exports` to `{".": "./src/index.ts"}` and forbids build scripts — so the transform supplies them from here. Each entry is vendored verbatim from the upstream manifest named in `provenance`, never rewritten from intuition, because the `files` lists in particular encode which test, fixture and harness files must stay out of a tarball. `@lostgradient/cinder` is the one exception: COR-1186 ruled that its 992-key map is regenerated by `cinder/generate-exports.ts`, so its `exports` and `files` carry the marker `{ "generator": "cinder" }` instead of literal values. `manifestFields` carries the top-level manifest keys a published package needs beyond its exports map: `main`, `module` and `types` for `moduleResolution: node10` consumers that never read `exports`, `publishConfig` (without `access: public` a scoped first publish is rejected outright) and `engines`. COR-1223 narrowed when those apply. `manifestFields` and `peerDependencies` are, as the sentence above says, vendored from the upstream manifest — so where the target still carries the key, the target holds the authoritative copy of the same fact and keeps it; `applySurfaceToManifest` supplies them only for a package the target does not have. `exports`, `files`, `bin` and `sideEffects` are unaffected and still written every run, because those are recomputed from corvidae's source and gated against the registry baseline rather than copied. `build.scripts` merge into the target's `scripts` block instead of replacing it, and `build.toolchain` skips any package the manifest already declares.

build.policy: `scripts` are the build-related manifest scripts, verbatim. `toolchain` names the packages the build command needs that corvidae's own manifest does not already declare; a `catalog:` value routes through the target root catalog where the target has one and is inlined where it does not. `requiredInputs` names the files the build command reads which corvidae does not carry — upstream's `scripts/build.ts`, `tsdown.config.ts` and the like. Those files live in the target repository and survive a sync because the transform never prunes, but nothing yet asserts they are present; `assertBuildInputsPresent` does that when a target clone is supplied. `sourceRoot` is the directory a `dist/` target maps back to when checking that the source a build would compile actually exists; it is `src/lib` for chat and editor, whose published trees are rooted one level deeper, and `src` everywhere else. `packedBy` records what actually produces the tarball. `files` means npm reads the allowlist directly, so every exports target must be covered by it. `pack-script` means the package stages its tarball through `scripts/pack-for-publish.ts`, which rewrites source conditions to their `dist` equivalents before packing — the four packages in the cinder repository do this, which is why their repository manifests legitimately carry `./src/**` targets the allowlist does not publish.

scripts.prepack: bun run build && bun run verify:exports && bun run verify:portability && bun run validate:package-consumers

scripts.prepublishOnly: bun run validate && bun run build
scripts.clean: rm -rf dist coverage tsconfig.tsbuildinfo lostgradient-cinder-*.tgz cinder-*.tgz tmp fixtures/node-consumer/node_modules fixtures/node-consumer/dist fixtures/sveltekit-consumer/node_modules fixtures/sveltekit-consumer/.svelte-kit fixtures/sveltekit-consumer/build fixtures/manifest-consumer/node_modules fixtures/typescript-consumer/node_modules fixtures/typescript-consumer/src/generated fixtures/examples-consumer/node_modules fixtures/examples-consumer/.svelte-kit fixtures/examples-consumer/build fixtures/examples-consumer/src/generated fixtures/examples-consumer/src/routes/+page.svelte

openQuestions: `requiredInputs` records that no build script in this list exists in corvidae. COR-1190 ruled that they stay target-owned rather than becoming transform-owned: the transform never prunes, so a file the target already carries survives every sync, and making the mirror author another repository’s build toolchain would put the mirror in charge of how the target builds. What changed is that the assumption is now checked — `assertBuildInputsPresent` in `sync.ts` fails a sync, naming every missing file, when a clone lacks one — so a manifest whose `build` script points at a file nothing wrote can no longer reach a publish silently.

`toolchain` is derived from the import closure of each upstream build entrypoint, not from the upstream `devDependencies` block as a whole. A build that shells out to a tool it never imports would be missed.
